subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Counting particles by mass: the mole
themeLabel: Models of the particulate nature of matter
bigPicture: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in moles: fixed, enormous batches of 6.02 × 10²³. The mole links what you can weigh or measure (mass, solution volume, gas volume) to the number of particles that actually react.

keyIdeas.answer: The SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly NA = 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formula units: always say which). Number of particles N = n × NA.

Masses compared with 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom. Mr = sum of the Ar values in the formula, using the booklet's two-decimal values. Both have no units. Example: Mr(H₂SO₄) = 2(1.01) + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = 98.09.

keyIdeas.cue: How are mass, moles and molar mass linked?
keyIdeas.answer: Molar mass M has units g mol⁻¹ and the same number as Mr. n = m/M. Chain: mass ↔ moles ↔ number of particles (× or ÷ NA).

keyIdeas.cue: Empirical vs molecular formula: how do you find them?
keyIdeas.answer: Empirical = simplest whole-number ratio; molecular = actual numbers of atoms. From % by mass: assume 100 g, divide each mass by Ar, divide by the smallest, round or scale to whole numbers. Molecular formula = empirical × (M ÷ empirical-formula mass).
c = n/V with V in dm³, units mol dm⁻³; square brackets mean concentration, e.g. [NaOH]. g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M. Remember 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Dilution keeps moles constant: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.

keyIdeas.cue: What is Avogadro's law and how is it used?
keyIdeas.answer: Equal volumes of any gases at the same temperature and pressure hold the same number of molecules. So for gases, volume ratios equal mole ratios: in N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 10 cm³ N₂ reacts with 30 cm³ H₂ to give 20 cm³ NH₃.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you get an empirical formula from combustion data?
keyIdeas.answer: All the C ends up in CO₂ and all the H in H₂O: mass of C = mass CO₂ × 12.01/44.01; mass of H = mass H₂O × 2.02/18.02. Any oxygen is found by difference from the sample mass. Change each mass to an amount in mol and divide by the smallest; multiply ratios ending in .5 by 2, .33 or .67 by 3, .25 or .75 by 4.

keyIdeas.cue: Serial or parallel dilution for a set of standards?
keyIdeas.answer: Serial: each solution is made from the previous one (e.g. 1:10 each time), useful for wide ranges but errors carry forward. Parallel: each standard is made directly from the stock. If a calculation needs a volume too small for your pipette, make an intermediate dilution first.

keyTerms.def: Amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ specified particles.
Mass of one mole of a substance, g mol⁻¹.
Actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
Amount of solute per dm³ of solution, mol dm⁻³.
Water bonded within a hydrated salt's lattice, e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O.

workedExamples.title: Empirical to molecular formula
workedExamples.prompt: A compound is 85.6% C and 14.4% H by mass, M = 56.1 g mol⁻¹. Find both formulas.

workedExamples.title: Concentration conversion
workedExamples.prompt: What mass of Na₂CO₃ (M = 105.99 g mol⁻¹) is needed for 250.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution?

misconceptions.right: It contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and three times as many atoms (1.81 × 10²⁴).

misconceptions.wrong: Volume in cm³ goes straight into n = cV.
misconceptions.right: Divide cm³ by 1000 to get dm³ first.

misconceptions.wrong: Empirical-formula ratios like 1 : 1.5 can be rounded to 1 : 2.
misconceptions.right: Multiply up: 1 : 1.5 becomes 2 : 3. Round only values within about 0.1 of a whole number.

misconceptions.wrong: Percentage composition only works from data to formula.
misconceptions.right: You also need the reverse: % by mass of an element = (number of atoms × Ar ÷ Mr) × 100.

practice.prompt: Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in 4.40 g of CO₂ (M = 44.01 g mol⁻¹).
A hydrated salt MgSO₄·xH₂O loses 51.2% of its mass on heating to constant mass. Determine x (M MgSO₄ = 120.38, H₂O = 18.02).
checkpoints: Per 100 g: 48.8 g MgSO₄ = 0.405 mol; 51.2 g H₂O = 2.84 mol

practice.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl is diluted to 500.0 cm³. Calculate the new concentration.

paper1A.stem: How many moles of ions are in 0.10 mol of Al₂(SO₄)₃?
paper1A.why: Each formula unit gives 2 Al³⁺ + 3 SO₄²⁻ = 5 ions.

paper1A.stem: What is the empirical formula of a compound with molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆?
What volume of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH contains 0.010 mol?
At the same T and p, 20 cm³ of CH₄ is burned: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l). What volume of O₂ reacts?

paper1B.data: Heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate. Crucible 20.00 g; crucible + hydrated salt 22.50 g; crucible after heating to constant mass 21.60 g. M(CuSO₄) = 159.62, M(H₂O) = 18.02.
paper1B.prompt: Determine x in CuSO₄·xH₂O and suggest why heating to constant mass matters.
paper1B.answer: Anhydrous 1.60 g = 0.01002 mol; water 0.90 g = 0.0499 mol; ratio ≈ 5, so x = 5. Constant mass shows all water has been driven off; otherwise x comes out too low.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: Convert cm³ to dm³; keep 3 significant figures and do not round mid-calculation.
Say which particle you are counting: molecules, atoms or ions.
Use two-decimal Ar values from the booklet (Cl 35.45, not 35.5) unless the question gives values.
Show each step with units; method marks are often given even if the final answer slips.
